checkpoint.question: In an interview, what is the best rule of thumb for deciding between inheritance and composition?
options: Ask 'Does class B genuinely have an IS-A relationship with class A in every conceivable context?' If yes, use inheritance; otherwise, use composition (HAS-A)
Always use inheritance because it requires fewer lines of code
Always use composition because inheritance has been removed from Java
Use inheritance for public classes and composition for private classes
checkpoint.explanation: Only use inheritance if B genuinely is an A and every method of A makes sense on B. In all other cases, wrap A inside B as a component (composition) and forward necessary calls.

checkpoint.question: Why is mastering equals(), hashCode(), and toString() critical for every Java developer?
options: Because they define how objects are compared, hashed in collections like HashMap/HashSet, and formatted for logging and debugging
Because without overriding them, Java programs cannot compile
Because they are the only three methods allowed in the Object class
Because they execute in native C++ machine code
checkpoint.explanation: Every class in Java inherits equals(), hashCode(), and toString() from java.lang.Object. Proper implementation is necessary for value comparison, collection hashing, and readable diagnostics.

pages.title: 1. Prerequisite check
pages.content: Before starting **equals, hashCode and toString**, recall the Java syntax and object/model concepts required for it. Write down what you already know, then identify one question you cannot yet answer confidently. The purpose of this step is to expose a missing prerequisite before new material is introduced.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 1. prerequisite check for equals, hashCode and toString.

checkpoint.question: What is the default implementation of equals() provided by java.lang.Object?
options: Reference identity comparison (this == obj), returning true only if both references point to the exact same heap memory address
Comparing all fields byte-by-byte
Comparing the class names lexicographically
Always returning true
checkpoint.explanation: By default, Object.equals(Object obj) simply performs 'this == obj'. Unless overridden, two distinct instances with identical field values are considered NOT equal.

pages.title: 2. Build the concept
pages.content: equals, hashCode and toString should be learned through a progression from terminology and mental model to tracing, implementation, and independent application. Start with the rule, then connect the rule to one small Java example. Avoid memorizing a code template before you can explain why each important line is present.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 2. build the concept for equals, hashCode and toString.

checkpoint.question: What is the mandatory contract between equals() and hashCode() in Java?
options: If two objects are equal according to equals(), they MUST have the same hashCode() value
If two objects have the same hashCode(), they must be equal according to equals()
hashCode() must always return a negative integer
equals() and hashCode() cannot be overridden in the same class
checkpoint.explanation: The contract mandates: if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() MUST equal b.hashCode(). The reverse is NOT required (hash collisions are permitted, though distinct hash codes improve performance).

pages.title: 3. Build a mental model
pages.content: Imagine the runtime state while **equals, hashCode and toString** executes. Identify the important actors, ownership, values, references, control flow, or exception paths. Explain the relationship in plain language before touching a full program.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 3. build a mental model for equals, hashCode and toString.

checkpoint.question: How does a HashMap use hashCode() and equals() to look up a key?
options: It calls hashCode() to calculate the array bucket index, then calls equals() on entries in that bucket to find the exact key match
It compares all keys using equals() sequentially in O(N) time without using hashCode()
It sorts all keys using toString()
It queries the operating system registry
checkpoint.explanation: HashMap hashes the key to locate the bucket in O(1) time. If multiple keys hash to the same bucket (collision), it traverses the bucket bucket using equals() to find the exact key match.

pages.title: 4. Worked example

pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 4. worked example for equals, hashCode and toString.

checkpoint.question: In an idiomatic equals() implementation, what is the first check that should be performed for performance?
options: if (this == obj) return true; (checking reference identity)
if (obj == null) throw new NullPointerException();
this.hashCode() == obj.hashCode()
this.toString().equals(obj.toString())
checkpoint.explanation: Checking 'if (this == obj) return true;' is an optimal performance shortcut: if both references point to the same object, field-by-field comparison can be skipped entirely.

pages.title: 5. Dry run before execution

pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 5. dry run before execution for equals, hashCode and toString.

checkpoint.question: What does Objects.hash(id, name, salary) compute behind the scenes in Java?
options: It combines the hash codes of each argument into a single 32-bit integer using a multiplier (traditionally 31)
It returns the memory address of the first parameter
It encrypts the parameters with SHA-256
It returns the number of non-null arguments
checkpoint.explanation: java.util.Objects.hash(...) creates an array and delegates to Arrays.hashCode(), iteratively multiplying by 31 and adding each element's hashCode to distribute hash values evenly.

checkpoint.question: What is the recommended signature when overriding the equals method?
options: public boolean equals(Object obj) (accepting java.lang.Object)
public boolean equals(Employee obj) (overloading with specific type)
public void equals(Object obj)
public static boolean equals(Object a, Object b)
checkpoint.explanation: equals must accept java.lang.Object (public boolean equals(Object obj)). Writing equals(Employee obj) is an overload, not an override, and will NOT be invoked by Collections like HashSet or HashMap!

checkpoint.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five equivalence relation requirements for equals() defined in Java SE specifications?
options: Asynchronous: equals() must run in a separate background thread
Reflexive: x.equals(x) must return true
Symmetric: x.equals(y) returns true if and only if y.equals(x) returns true
Transitive: if x.equals(y) and y.equals(z), then x.equals(z) must return true
checkpoint.explanation: The five mathematical equivalence requirements for Object.equals() are: Reflexive, Symmetric, Transitive, Consistent, and Non-nullity (x.equals(null) returns false). Asynchrony is not a requirement.

checkpoint.question: What catastrophe occurs if a class overrides equals() but fails to override hashCode() when used in a HashSet?
options: Equal objects will produce different hash codes and be placed into different buckets, causing set.contains() to return false for an object that is logically present
The compiler throws a ClassFormatError
The HashSet immediately throws an UnsupportedOperationException
The JVM crashes with a segmentation fault
checkpoint.explanation: If hashCode() is not overridden, equal objects inherit different identity hash codes from Object. HashSet will search the wrong bucket and fail to find the object, violating set uniqueness.

checkpoint.question: Why should mutable fields never be used in hashCode() calculations if the object is used as a key in a HashMap?
options: Mutating the field changes the object's hashCode, leaving it trapped in its original bucket and making it impossible to retrieve using get()
HashMap will throw a ConcurrentModificationException immediately upon field mutation
The field value will be reverted to its default value
The JVM will disable garbage collection for that object
checkpoint.explanation: If a key's hashCode changes after being added to a HashMap, future lookups compute the new bucket index and look in the wrong slot, rendering the key-value pair permanently lost.

checkpoint.question: What is the primary purpose of overriding toString() in custom Java classes?
options: To provide a clear, informative, human-readable string representation of the object's state for logging and debugging
To convert the object into JSON for HTTP transmission automatically
To serialize the object bytes to disk
To define the object's unique database primary key

topics.description: Learn Immutability and Defensive Copying through step-by-step concept building, worked Java examples, dry runs, guided labs, independent practice and mastery checks.

pages.title: Step-by-step learning path
pages.content: Follow this exact sequence for **Immutability and Defensive Copying**: prerequisite check → concept build → mental model → worked example → dry run → guided implementation → independent practice → mastery gate. Do not skip to the final practice set until the guided implementation is understood.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete step-by-step learning path for Immutability and Defensive Copying.

checkpoint.question: What is an immutable object in Java?
options: An object whose state (data) cannot be modified after it has been constructed
An object that cannot be garbage collected
An object with only static methods
An object declared inside an abstract class
checkpoint.explanation: An immutable object guarantees that its observable state remains strictly constant throughout its entire lifetime after initialization. Java's String and Integer classes are classic examples.

pages.title: 1. Prerequisite check
pages.content: Before starting **Immutability and Defensive Copying**, recall the Java syntax and object/model concepts required for it. Write down what you already know, then identify one question you cannot yet answer confidently. The purpose of this step is to expose a missing prerequisite before new material is introduced.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 1. prerequisite check for Immutability and Defensive Copying.

checkpoint.question: Why does declaring a reference variable as 'final' NOT automatically make the referenced object immutable?
options: final only prevents the reference variable from pointing to another object; the internal fields of the referenced object can still be mutated
final is ignored by the Java compiler at runtime
final only applies to primitive numbers
final forces the object to be cloned on every read
checkpoint.explanation: A final reference (e.g. final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>()) cannot be reassigned, but the underlying object itself is completely mutable (e.g. list.add("item") works freely).

pages.title: 2. Build the concept
pages.content: Immutability and Defensive Copying should be learned through a progression from terminology and mental model to tracing, implementation, and independent application. Start with the rule, then connect the rule to one small Java example. Avoid memorizing a code template before you can explain why each important line is present.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 2. build the concept for Immutability and Defensive Copying.

checkpoint.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the 5 rules for creating an immutable class in Java?
options: Provide public setter methods for all fields
Declare the class as final so it cannot be extended
Make all fields private and final
Do not provide any mutator methods and perform defensive copying on mutable components
checkpoint.explanation: An immutable class must NEVER provide mutator methods (setters). The 5 rules are: (1) no setters, (2) final class, (3) private final fields, (4) exclusive access to mutable components, (5) defensive copying.

pages.title: 3. Build a mental model
pages.content: Imagine the runtime state while **Immutability and Defensive Copying** executes. Identify the important actors, ownership, values, references, control flow, or exception paths. Explain the relationship in plain language before touching a full program.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 3. build a mental model for Immutability and Defensive Copying.

checkpoint.question: Why are immutable objects inherently thread-safe in concurrent multi-threaded programs?
options: Because multiple threads can read their state concurrently without any risk of data races or corruption, eliminating the need for locks or synchronization
Because the JVM forces threads to take turns accessing immutable objects
Because immutable objects execute on the main thread only
Because immutable objects are stored in thread-local CPU registers
checkpoint.explanation: Race conditions and synchronization bugs occur when multiple threads concurrently read and write shared mutable state. Since immutable objects can never be mutated, they are inherently thread-safe for reading.

pages.title: 4. Worked example
pages.content: Take one small example for **Immutability and Defensive Copying** and solve it in visible steps: state the input, apply the first rule, update the state, and predict the output or effect. Then compare your reasoning with the executable example in this topic.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 4. worked example for Immutability and Defensive Copying.

checkpoint.question: In an immutable Period class with fields start and end (of type java.util.Date), why must the constructor perform defensive copying?
options: Because Date is mutable; without defensive copying, the caller could retain a reference to the passed Date and modify Period's internal dates externally
Because Date objects cannot be stored in final fields
Because java.util.Date throws an exception if not copied
Because the constructor cannot assign values to Date fields directly
checkpoint.explanation: java.util.Date is mutable. If the constructor does this.start = start;, the caller still holds a pointer to start and can call start.setYear(...), corrupting Period's invariant that start <= end.

pages.title: 5. Dry run before execution
pages.content: Trace the program line by line using a state table. Record changed variables, object fields, references, collections, thread state, or exception flow. The goal is to make the execution predictable rather than mysterious.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 5. dry run before execution for Immutability and Defensive Copying.

checkpoint.question: In defensive copying, what is the 'Time of Check to Time of Use' (TOCTOU) vulnerability avoided by copying parameters BEFORE checking invariants?
options: Another thread could mutate the parameter object between the moment validity was verified and the moment it was assigned, so copying first ensures validation runs on the private copy
The system clock changing during execution
Garbage collection deleting the parameters
Compilation delays exceeding 100 milliseconds
checkpoint.explanation: In multi-threaded environments, if you check parameters first and copy second, another thread could alter the object between the check and copy. Always copy first, then validate the cloned copy.

pages.content: Implement a minimal version of **Immutability and Defensive Copying** using the starter structure supplied in the practice problem. First fill in the missing concept, then run the smallest sample, then expand to a second case. Do not optimize before the behavior is correct.

checkpoint.question: When writing a getter for a mutable component field (e.g. getScores() returning int[]), how must the getter be implemented in an immutable class?
options: return scores.clone(); (return a defensive copy of the array)
return scores; (return direct reference)
return null;
throw new UnsupportedOperationException();
checkpoint.explanation: Returning a direct reference to internal array scores allows callers to write getScores()[0] = 999, corrupting the instance. Returning scores.clone() protects the internal array.

pages.title: 7. Independent practice

pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 7. independent practice for Immutability and Defensive Copying.

checkpoint.question: What is an optimization advantage of immutable objects regarding caching hash codes?
options: Because fields never change, the hashCode() can be precomputed or lazily computed once and cached in an instance field for fast repeated lookups
Immutable objects do not need a hashCode() method
Hash codes of immutable objects are always 0
The JVM stores all immutable objects in CPU registers
checkpoint.explanation: Java's String class caches its hashCode in an internal field (hash). Since String is immutable, the hash code is calculated once and reused for all subsequent HashMap lookups.

checkpoint.question: What is the primary trade-off or downside of using immutable objects?
options: Every state change requires allocating a separate, new object on the heap, which can cause memory churn and GC pressure in tight loops
Immutable objects cannot be passed as method arguments
Immutable classes cannot implement interfaces
Immutable objects can only be created in Java 21
checkpoint.explanation: Modifying an immutable object requires constructing a new object holding the updated value. In tight loops (like appending strings), this causes high object allocation overhead (which is why StringBuilder exists).

checkpoint.question: What mistake is made when declaring: private final List<String> items; and returning Collections.unmodifiableList(items) without defensive copying in the constructor?
options: The caller who created the original List passed to the constructor can still add elements to it, modifying the 'unmodifiable' list view indirectly
unmodifiableList() throws an exception if the list has fewer than 10 elements
The items list is deleted from memory
The class cannot be instantiated
checkpoint.explanation: Collections.unmodifiableList(original) is just a wrapper view. If the caller still holds a reference to original, modifying original will be reflected in the unmodifiable wrapper. A defensive copy is required: new ArrayList<>(original).

checkpoint.question: Why does modern Java recommend using java.time types (LocalDate, Instant) instead of legacy java.util.Date?

java.util.Date only works in the Pacific timezone
java.time classes do not require memory
java.util.Date cannot represent years past 2025

checkpoint.question: What is the purpose of modern Java object models such as enum, record, and sealed types?
options: To provide concise, expressive, type-safe constructs that model domain data with minimal boilerplate and strong compiler guarantees
To replace the JVM with a WebAssembly compiler
To deprecate all standard Java classes and interfaces
To allow Java code to run without memory allocation
checkpoint.explanation: Modern Java features (enums, records in Java 16, sealed types in Java 17) eliminate boilerplate while giving the compiler rich semantic knowledge for pattern matching and type exhaustiveness.

checkpoint.question: What tedious boilerplate code is automatically generated when you define a Java record (e.g. record Point(int x, int y) {})?
options: Private final fields, canonical constructor, public accessors (x(), y()), equals(), hashCode(), and toString()
Public setters, XML serializers, and database tables
Static factory methods and thread pool executors
A main() method and unit test suite
checkpoint.explanation: A Java record automatically creates private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessors matching field names, equals(), hashCode(), and a descriptive toString() in a single line of code.

checkpoint.question: Which of the following is true about Java records?
options: Records are implicitly final and cannot extend any other class because they already extend java.lang.Record
Records can extend abstract classes
Record fields are mutable and have setter methods
Records cannot implement interfaces
checkpoint.explanation: All records are implicitly final and cannot be extended. They implicitly inherit from java.lang.Record, meaning they cannot extend another class, although they can implement interfaces.

checkpoint.question: What is a Java enum behind the scenes in bytecode?
options: A specialized final class extending java.lang.Enum, with each enum constant represented as a public static final instance of that class
A simple integer type identical to C enums
A dynamic JSON dictionary loaded at runtime
A primitive data type stored on the stack
checkpoint.explanation: In Java, an enum is a full-featured class extending java.lang.Enum. Each declared constant is a public static final singleton instance instantiated once when the enum class loads.

checkpoint.question: What is a 'compact constructor' in a Java record?
options: A constructor without parameter lists used specifically to validate or normalize arguments before field assignment (e.g. public Range { if (start > end) throw...; })
A constructor that compresses object memory using GZIP
A constructor that takes no parameters
A private constructor that prevents record creation
checkpoint.explanation: A compact constructor in a record omits the parameter list entirely (e.g. public Point { ... }). It allows validating or modifying parameters before the compiler automatically assigns them to fields.

checkpoint.question: How does pattern matching for switch work with sealed types in modern Java (Java 17+ / 21)?
options: Because the compiler knows all permitted subclasses of the sealed type, it can verify exhaustiveness at compile time, eliminating the need for a default branch
It requires a default branch in every switch statement
It only works with primitive integers
It executes pattern matching asynchronously
checkpoint.explanation: Sealed classes explicitly declare their permitted subtypes. When switching over a sealed hierarchy, if all permitted types are covered, the compiler verifies exhaustiveness without needing a default branch.

No, enums can only contain names without data or methods
Yes, but only if all fields are static integers
No, enums cannot have constructors

checkpoint.question: Why does the compiler prevent declaring public constructors in a Java enum?
options: Enums represent fixed, compile-time singletons; external callers cannot be allowed to create new instances at runtime with 'new'
Because enums are stored in read-only Metaspace memory
Because public constructors are reserved for records only
To allow JVM garbage collection to delete enums

checkpoint.question: In an interview, when would you choose a record over a standard class?

When fields need to change values dynamically after creation
When writing database entity classes with JPA/Hibernate that require no-arg constructors and setters

Imports, Class Body, Main Method

+ is integer, - is string, # is double, and ~ is boolean

Aggregation uses an arrow; Composition has no connector

pages.title: Guided Checkpoint 1
pages.content: A constructor has the same name as its class and has no return type. It runs when an object is created and is commonly used to initialize object state.

checkpoint.question: What is the defining property of a Java constructor?
options: It has the same name as its class and no return type
It must return int
It is always static
It can be inherited unchanged

pages.title: Why this concept matters
pages.content: Constructors establish valid initial object state at the moment of creation. Good constructors reduce scattered initialization and clarify what an object requires.
pages.teachingGoal: Explain why Constructor in Java matters in real Java programs and identify when the concept is appropriate.

checkpoint.question: Why are constructors essential for writing robust, fail-safe Java code?
options: They guarantee that an object cannot come into existence in an invalid, incomplete, or corrupted state
They speed up JVM class loading by 50%
They prevent the garbage collector from running
They automatically generate database schemas
checkpoint.explanation: Constructors enforce object invariants at the exact moment of creation by requiring necessary arguments and executing validation, ensuring half-baked or invalid objects cannot exist.

A subclass overriding a superclass constructor
checkpoint.explanation: Constructor overloading allows a class to have multiple constructors differing in the number, type, or order of parameters (e.g. no-arg, default-values, full-initialization).

It compiles and acts as the default constructor
The compiler throws a SyntaxError: 'classes cannot have methods with class name'
The program crashes immediately upon launch

topics.title: Inheritance in Java
topics.description: Learn Inheritance in Java through focused explanations and practical Java examples. Learn through structured explanations, worked examples, dry runs, guided practice, and mastery checks.

pages.title: What is Inheritance
pages.content: Inheritance allows a subclass to reuse members of a superclass with the `extends` keyword. A subclass can directly use inherited methods and add its own behavior.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend superclass behavior.

checkpoint.question: Which feature allows a subclass to provide its own implementation of an inherited method?
options: Method overriding
Method hiding of fields
Constructor overloading
Variable declaration
checkpoint.explanation: Method overriding lets a subclass redefine an inherited instance method.

pages.title: What is Polymorphism
pages.content: Polymorphism allows a superclass reference to refer to a subclass object. With method overriding, the subclass implementation is selected at runtime.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Overridden methods enable runtime polymorphism.

checkpoint.question: Given: Animal a = new Dog(); a.makeSound(); (where Dog extends Animal and overrides makeSound()) Which version of makeSound() is executed?
options: Dog's overridden makeSound() method, due to runtime dynamic method dispatch
Animal's original makeSound() method, because reference 'a' is of type Animal
Both methods run simultaneously
Compilation error because types do not match
checkpoint.explanation: Java uses dynamic method dispatch for instance methods: the actual method executed is determined at runtime based on the actual object instance (Dog), not the reference type (Animal).

pages.title: Why this concept matters
pages.content: Inheritance models an is-a relationship and enables reuse plus specialization. Polymorphism then lets parent references work with child objects.
pages.teachingGoal: Explain why Inheritance in Java matters in real Java programs and identify when the concept is appropriate.
pages.suggestedVisual: Animal -> Mammal -> Dog tree plus runtime dispatch arrow.

checkpoint.question: What is the primary benefit of polymorphism when writing scalable, maintainable Java systems?
options: Client code can work uniformly with superclass or interface types without needing to know or change when new subclasses are added (Open/Closed Principle)
It removes the need for object allocation in heap memory
It replaces loops with automatic recursion
It compiles Java code directly to native x86 machine code
checkpoint.explanation: Polymorphism enables the Open/Closed Principle: code can be open for extension but closed for modification. You can introduce new subclasses without modifying the client code that operates on the supertype.

checkpoint.question: What does the 'super' keyword do when invoked as super() inside a subclass constructor?
options: It invokes the constructor of the immediate superclass to initialize inherited fields
It reboots the Java Virtual Machine
It grants superuser administrative privileges to the class
It casts the object to the top-level Object class
checkpoint.explanation: super() invokes the superclass constructor. If not written explicitly, the Java compiler automatically inserts a call to super() as the first statement of any subclass constructor.

checkpoint.question: Why should developers always annotate overridden methods with the @Override annotation in Java?
options: It causes the compiler to verify that the method actually overrides a superclass method, catching misspelled names or mismatched parameter types at compile time
It makes the method execute 2x faster in the JIT compiler
It is required by the JVM bytecode verifier
It makes the method accessible to all packages
checkpoint.explanation: @Override is a compiler safety check. If you accidentally misspell the method name (e.g. tostring() instead of toString()) or get parameters wrong, the compiler flags an error immediately.

checkpoint.question: When creating a subclass object: new Dog(), what is the order of constructor execution?
options: Object constructor -> Animal constructor -> Dog constructor (top of inheritance hierarchy down to the leaf)
Dog constructor -> Animal constructor -> Object constructor
Dog constructor only; superclass constructors do not run
Animal constructor and Dog constructor run in parallel
checkpoint.explanation: Constructors execute base-to-derived: superclass constructors must complete before subclass constructor logic runs, ensuring base state is fully established before specialized fields are initialized.

pages.title: Common mistakes and debugging
pages.content:
- **Mistake:** Using inheritance for has-a relationships
  **Fix:** state the rule, isolate the smallest failing input, and rerun the corrected case.
- **Mistake:** Changing the method signature accidentally
  **Fix:** state the rule, isolate the smallest failing input, and rerun the corrected case.
- **Mistake:** Expecting a parent reference to expose child-only methods
  **Fix:** state the rule, isolate the smallest failing input, and rerun the corrected case.
pages.teachingGoal: Diagnose common mistakes in Inheritance in Java and fix them using the underlying Java rule.

checkpoint.question: What common architectural error occurs when a developer uses inheritance instead of composition?
options: Subclassing a class just to reuse a single helper method, creating an inappropriate IS-A relationship that exposes unwanted superclass methods
Declaring too many interfaces
Making instance variables private
Writing more than one constructor in a class
checkpoint.explanation: Inheritance creates an unbreakable IS-A bond. Using inheritance merely for code reuse (e.g. Car extending Engine) exposes irrelevant methods and causes fragile hierarchies; composition should be used instead.

pages.content:

pages.teachingGoal: Use the mastery review to explain, implement, test, and debug Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: Does Java support multiple inheritance of classes (e.g. class C extends A, B)? Why or why not?
options: No, Java does not support multiple class inheritance to avoid the Diamond Problem and architectural complexity; classes can only extend one superclass
Yes, Java supports multiple inheritance for classes using commas
Yes, but only if all classes are in the same package
No, Java classes cannot inherit from any class
checkpoint.explanation: Java disallows multiple class inheritance to prevent ambiguity (the Diamond Problem) where two parents define the same method with different implementations. Java supports multiple interface implementation instead.

pages.title: Why this concept matters
pages.content: Integrated OOP practice is where class design stops being isolated syntax and becomes a way to model a small domain cleanly.
pages.teachingGoal: Explain why Practice matters in real Java programs and identify when the concept is appropriate.
pages.suggestedVisual: Requirement -> classes -> relationships -> methods -> objects workflow.

checkpoint.question: What is the ultimate goal of integrated Object-Oriented design practice?
options: Synthesizing classes, encapsulation, constructors, and polymorphism into cohesive, loosely coupled domain models that solve real-world problems cleanly
Writing the maximum number of classes possible in a single project
Memorizing all Java keywords without writing code
Eliminating all functions from software systems
checkpoint.explanation: Integrated practice transitions the developer from memorizing isolated syntax rules to applying sound design principles (cohesion, encapsulation, separation of concerns) in real systems.

pages.title: Core ideas and vocabulary
pages.content:
- **Class design:** define it, identify when to use it, and connect it to a concrete Java rule or API.
- **Constructor reuse:** define it, identify when to use it, and connect it to a concrete Java rule or API.
- **Inheritance:** define it, identify when to use it, and connect it to a concrete Java rule or API.
- **Overriding:** define it, identify when to use it, and connect it to a concrete Java rule or API.
- **Polymorphism:** define it, identify when to use it, and connect it to a concrete Java rule or API.
pages.teachingGoal: Define the core vocabulary of Practice and connect each term to a concrete Java example.

checkpoint.question: What does the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) dictate for class design in Java?
options: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change, meaning it should focus on a single cohesive responsibility or domain concern
A class can only contain a single method
A class can only be instantiated once in the JVM
A class can only be modified by a single developer
checkpoint.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle (the 'S' in SOLID) states that each class should encapsulate a single specific responsibility. Mixing concerns (e.g. database access, business rules, and UI formatting in one class) makes software fragile.

pages.title: Worked examples

pages.teachingGoal: Use worked examples to predict program behavior for Practice before execution.

checkpoint.question: In an e-commerce model with classes Cart, CartItem, Product, and PricingService, how should responsibilities be separated?
options: Product holds item details; CartItem links Product to quantity; Cart manages the list of items; PricingService computes discounts and tax
All fields and calculations should be placed inside a single 2,000-line Cart class
Product should directly query the database and send customer emails
CartItem should inherit from PricingService and Cart
checkpoint.explanation: Separating responsibilities into distinct domain entities (Product, CartItem, Cart) and domain services (PricingService) maintains clean boundaries and high cohesion.

pages.title: Dry run: track the state
pages.content: A strong Java learner can explain how state changes line by line. Trace the variable, object field, collection content, or exception path before executing the program.
pages.teachingGoal: Dry-run Practice by tracking program state line by line.

checkpoint.question: When dry-running a complex multi-class interaction, why is drawing an object interaction diagram or sequence diagram helpful?
options: It visualizes how messages (method calls) flow between collaborating objects and how object states evolve over time
It compiles the Java source code automatically
It prevents the computer from running out of disk space
It is required by the Java garbage collector
checkpoint.explanation: Sequence and interaction diagrams map out runtime messaging between objects, making it clear which object initiates actions and how states change across method invocations.

pages.title: Common mistakes and debugging
pages.content:
- **Mistake:** Putting all state in one class
  **Fix:** state the rule, isolate the smallest failing input, and rerun the corrected case.
- **Mistake:** Duplicating parent fields in every child
  **Fix:** state the rule, isolate the smallest failing input, and rerun the corrected case.
- **Mistake:** Creating deep inheritance when composition would be clearer
  **Fix:** state the rule, isolate the smallest failing input, and rerun the corrected case.
pages.teachingGoal: Diagnose common mistakes in Practice and fix them using the underlying Java rule.

checkpoint.question: What is an anti-pattern known as a 'God Class' (or Blob) in object-oriented programming?
options: A massive monolithic class that knows too much or does too much, accumulating dozens of unrelated fields and methods and centralizing all system logic
A class that inherits from java.lang.Object
A class that has a main() method
A class declared with the public modifier
checkpoint.explanation: A 'God Class' is a classic anti-pattern where a single oversized class controls too many unrelated responsibilities, reducing other classes to passive data holders and making the codebase hard to maintain.

pages.teachingGoal: Use the mastery review to explain, implement, test, and debug Practice.

checkpoint.question: Which of the following is a reliable indicator that an object-oriented design is well-structured?
options: High cohesion within classes, loose coupling between classes, explicit encapsulation of state, and code that is easy to unit-test in isolation
All fields are public so any class can access them without getters
Every class extends at least 5 superclasses
The entire program is written inside a single source file
checkpoint.explanation: The hallmarks of excellent object-oriented design are high cohesion (focused classes), loose coupling (minimal dependencies), strict encapsulation (data protection), and high testability.
